newsitem.title: ITALY: EU probes cheese scare, Italy's producers hit back.
newsitem.headline: EU probes cheese scare, Italy's producers hit back.

text.p: The European Commission on Tuesday said it was investigating a botulism scare in Italy linked to mascarpone cheese as producers accused the media of dramatising.

The alarm over the soft, sweet cheese, a main ingredient in many Italian desserts, follows the death of a 15-year-old boy in Naples and at least six other certified cases of botulism in southern Italy among people who had eaten mascarpone.
"A Commission official went to Italy to investigate," Commission spokesman Jean-Christophe Filori said in Brussels.
He said the official would return at the end of the week to report whether all necessary measures had been implemented.
If not, EU safeguard action may be taken, Filori said.

Under the EU rapid alert system, the Commission immediately notified countries to which the cheese was exported -- Belgium, Spain, Sweden and Austria -- after being informed by the Italian authorities, Filori told a briefing.

Belgium said on Monday it would withdraw all mascarpone sold under the Giglio, Parmalat and Sol di Valle brand names, while Sweden warned consumers not to eat those brands until more was known about the scare.
Health inspectors in Italy have pulled well over 100,000 tubs of mascarpone sold under the three names from store shelves, including 10,000 packs withdrawn on Monday.
Parmalat, one of Italy's main food producers, issued a statement on Tuesday saying that none of its products was linked to the "presumed bacterial poisoning".
It said it had financial control of Giglio but not of its production, management and commercial activities.
Botulism is a severe form of poisoning from foods that contain a toxin which can affect the central nervous system. In fatal cases, death is often caused by heart and lung failure.
The bacterium is most typically found in improperly preserved canned raw meat.

"Parmalat cautions against linking its name and its brand to issues that it do not concern it. Parmalat also states that no case of botulism poisoning has ever been verified in the world in milk and cheese products," a company statement said.
Italy's milk and cheese producers' association also said there was no precedent for botulism in such products. It said Italian media had ignored the facts and whipped up a scare.
"Such an attitude is to be condemned because it leads to unjustified collective psychosis and causes incalculable damage to all the productive sectors concerned," the association said.
